content: 1. The sensitivity of diagnostic tests for certain infections tends to be lower in women. 2. Culturing Chlamydia trachomatis requires highly skilled laboratories and technicians due to the complexity, labor-intensive nature, and time-consuming process, making it economically impractical in most cases. This method is rarely performed in middleor high-income countries except for specific purposes. 3. Culturing Neisseria gonorrhoeae requires a specialized culture medium enriched with nutrients to support the organism's growth. Cervical and anorectal specimens can be used for this purpose. 4. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing is essential for guiding therapy, particularly in cases where N. gonorrhoeae isolates are resistant to standard recommended treatments. 5. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that individuals presenting with symptoms of vaginal discharge be treated for N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis, and/or Trichomonas vaginalis during the same visit. 6. WHO suggests basing treatment on the results of quality-assured molecular assays for N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis, and/or T. vaginalis when available. 7. In settings with access to quality-assured molecular assays and a fully operational quality management system, results should ideally be available on the same day to guide treatment decisions. 8. WHO recommends using self-collected or clinician-collected vaginal swabs or urine specimens for molecular testing to diagnose and treat N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis, and/or T. vaginalis. 9. If vaginal discharge is present, WHO suggests treating for bacterial vaginosis based on clinical findings (e.g., tenacious or thin discharge) or microscopy results, if available. 10. In settings where same-day molecular testing is not feasible, WHO suggests using quality-assured rapid tests with a minimum sensitivity of 80% and specificity of 90% to confirm or exclude infections with N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis. 11. If rapid tests or molecular assays are unavailable, WHO recommends performing a speculum examination and treating for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis if cervicitis is evident. For individuals with negative speculum findings but at high risk of infection, testing should be performed, and treatment should be based on the results. 12. In the absence of rapid tests and speculum examination, WHO suggests treating all individuals at high risk of sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and those with confirmed vaginal discharge. 13. For individuals with recurrent or persistent vaginal discharge, referral to a center with laboratory capacity to diagnose infections such as N. gonorrhoeae, C. trachomatis, Mycoplasma genitalium, T. vaginalis, and bacterial vaginosis is recommended. Testing for antimicrobial-resistant N. gonorrhoeae and M. genitalium should also be performed. 14. WHO emphasizes the importance of offering HIV and syphilis testing, as well as other preventive services, to individuals presenting with vaginal discharge. 15. Treatment for bacterial vaginosis and T. vaginalis can be achieved with the same medication, such as metronidazole. 16. For yeast infections like Candida albicans, treatment options include miconazole vaginal pessaries, clotrimazole vaginal tablets, or oral fluconazole. 17. Individuals taking metronidazole should avoid alcohol, and its use during the first trimester of pregnancy is not recommended unless the benefits outweigh the risks. 18. For cervical infections, first-line treatments for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis should be used, with substitutions or adjustments made based on local antimicrobial resistance data or patient-specific factors, such as pregnancy or breastfeeding. 19. Molecular assays or rapid point-of-care tests with high sensitivity and specificity are preferred for diagnosing and treating STIs, as they reduce missed cases and unnecessary treatments. 20. In settings where molecular assays are unavailable, strategies such as speculum examination or risk-based treatment can still reduce the incidence of pelvic inflammatory disease and unnecessary treatments, though they may be less accurate. 21. WHO guidelines provide flowcharts for healthcare providers and program managers to determine the most appropriate diagnostic and treatment strategies for vaginal discharge based on local resources and diagnostic capacity. 22. The use of diagnostic tests with high sensitivity and specificity not only improves treatment accuracy but also enhances understanding of STI prevalence, facilitates partner tracing, and improves overall quality of care.
